sections.section_title: Initial presentation: Capnocytophaga sepsis with DIC and multiorgan involvement
sections.description: Walks the reader through the timeline from dog bite to fulminant sepsis, outlining organism-specific considerations, early differential diagnoses, initial investigations, and immediate management decisions that framed the subsequent course.
subtopics: Dog bite exposure, missed outpatient antibiotics, and rapid clinical deterioration
Capnocytophaga canimorsus: reservoir, transmission routes, virulence, and slow culture growth implications
Sepsis physiology: hyperlactataemia, metabolic acidosis, refractory hypoglycaemia in severe infection
Initial laboratory profile: pancytopenia, coagulopathy, AKI, liver enzyme elevation
Early DIC vs severe sepsis: mottled extremities, microthrombotic skin/acrocyanotic changes
Empiric antibiotic rationale: piperacillin/tazobactam coverage for dog-associated flora; later de-escalation to ampicillin/penicillin after culture confirmation
ICU course: progression to anuria, septic cardiomyopathy, fluid overload, initiation of continuous renal replacement therapy
Early differentials considered: acute leukaemia, haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, necrotising soft-tissue infection (ruled out), autoimmune vasculitis (ANA/ANCA negative)
Supportive measures: blood product support (platelets, fibrinogen), albumin; hemodynamic monitoring without vasopressors beyond stress-dose steroids
Microbiology: delayed culture positivity for C. canimorsus and how this affects clinical decision-making

sections.section_title: Turning point: recognition of thrombotic microangiopathy after initial sepsis improvement
sections.description: Details the clinical inflection where isolated haemolysis and persistent thrombocytopenia emerged despite resolving sepsis/DIC, prompting reconsideration of the working diagnosis toward TMA.
subtopics: Clinical change on the ward: sudden haemoglobin drop without bleeding, persistently low platelets
Laboratory evidence of MAHA: undetectable haptoglobin, rising LDH, 15%–20% schistocytes on smear
DAT pitfalls: initial IgG-positive DAT (drug/transfusion-related false positivity), lack of steroid response, repeat DAT negative
Distinguishing DIC-related cytopenias from TMA: normalization of coagulation parameters yet ongoing haemolysis
When to perform kidney biopsy in suspected TMA: timing after platelet recovery and expected findings
Biopsy findings in this case: severe acute tubular necrosis, ischaemic glomeruli with fibrin thrombi, scattered crescents; absence of immune complex deposition on IF/EM

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of complement-mediated HUS and infectious triggers
sections.description: Provides the mechanistic basis for CM-HUS with emphasis on alternative complement pathway dysregulation, genetic predisposition versus acquired triggers, and how infections like C. canimorsus precipitate endothelial injury and TMA.
subtopics: Alternative complement pathway overview: tick-over, C3 convertase amplification, terminal pathway and MAC
Regulatory checkpoints: factor H, factor I, membrane cofactor protein (CD46); consequences of dysregulation
Genetic and autoimmune contributors: prevalence of pathogenic variants/anti–factor H antibodies and incomplete penetrance
Infection as a second hit: pregnancy, autoimmune disease, medications, and pathogens as triggers
Capnocytophaga–complement interaction: capsule-mediated serum resistance variability, complement as host defense, and the paradox of pathogen clearance vs endothelial injury
Why C3/C4 can be normal in CM-HUS and limitations of standard complement tests during active disease

sections.section_title: From differential to diagnosis: excluding mimics and confirming CM-HUS
sections.description: Explains the structured diagnostic approach used to rule out other TMAs and sepsis mimics, interpret specialized tests, and synthesize clinical, laboratory, and histopathologic data into a CM-HUS diagnosis.
subtopics: TTP first: using PLASMIC score for pretest stratification; ADAMTS13 activity threshold (<10% for TTP); patient’s ADAMTS13 at 43.5% argues against TTP
STEC-HUS exclusion: lack of diarrhoeal prodrome and negative stool PCR
Other secondary TMAs to consider and exclude: malignant hypertension, drugs, pregnancy/postpartum, autoimmune disease, transplant-associated TMA
Sepsis-associated DIC vs superimposed TMA: resolving coagulopathy with persistent MAHA and renal TMA on biopsy supports TMA
Complement evaluation strategy: roles and limitations of C3/C4, pathway assays (AH50), anti–factor H antibodies
Timing confounders: how plasma exchange and eculizumab alter functional complement assays (e.g., low AH50 post-therapy)
Genetic testing in CM-HUS: implications of negative results for prognosis and duration of complement blockade
Clinicopathologic synthesis: persistent haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, dialysis-dependent AKI, kidney biopsy with TMA, response to eculizumab

sections.section_title: Therapeutic strategy in infection-triggered CM-HUS: sequencing PEX, eculizumab, and supportive care
sections.description: Outlines the treatment rationale and logistics in the context of recent bacteraemia, including bridging plasma exchange, initiation of complement blockade, infection prevention, and organ support.
subtopics: Role of plasma exchange: lifesaving in TTP; transient benefit in CM-HUS; rationale for use as a bridge while awaiting diagnostics
Eculizumab: mechanism (C5 inhibition), timing (after culture negativity), induction and maintenance dosing used in the case
Vaccination and antimicrobial prophylaxis: MenACWY and MenB schedules; penicillin prophylaxis when vaccination timing is suboptimal; counselling on infection risks
Renal support: indications for CRRT; monitoring for return of diuresis and progression toward dialysis independence
Transfusion strategy: RBC support for symptomatic anaemia; platelet support individualized in the setting of TMA/DIC
Monitoring treatment response: platelets, LDH, haemoglobin stability, creatinine and urine output; tapering steroids after AIHA ruled out
Risk–benefit considerations: complement blockade in the setting of encapsulated organisms (Neisseria, Capnocytophaga) and mitigating strategies

sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s recovery trajectory and distills practical takeaways about recognition, workup, and timely therapy of CM-HUS precipitated by uncommon infections.
subtopics: Clinical outcome: return of urine output, partial renal recovery (creatinine ~175 µmol/L), dialysis independence
Hematologic remission on eculizumab and planned maintenance with reassessment for discontinuation
Impact of timing: earlier complement blockade associated with improved renal outcomes; delays risk incomplete recovery
Interpreting negative genetic testing: prognosis and decisions on duration of therapy and relapse surveillance
Key clinical pearls: consider CM-HUS when haemolysis emerges as sepsis resolves; normal C3/C4 do not exclude CM-HUS; peripheral smear is pivotal; biopsy supports diagnosis when safe

Broader implications: C. canimorsus as a rare CM-HUS trigger; value of early organism suspicion and molecular diagnostics for fastidious pathogens; infection-prevention protocols during complement inhibition
